title: Personal and family background
description: Corky Bush interviews Leah Brown in Teakean, Idaho on September 22, 1975, gathering biographical details. Brown, maiden name Martin, was born July 4, 1910 in Joplin, Missouri, moved to the Lenore area at nine and to a ranch near Teakean at fifteen.

title: The ranch; schooling; journey to Idaho
description: Brown describes the family ranch on the breaks above what is now Dworshak Dam and walking four miles through timber to South Teakean School, where she finished eighth grade. She recounts the trip from Missouri: the family's Maxwell car broke down in Wichita, Kansas, so she, her mother and brothers came on to Clarkston by train.

title: Parents' lives and work; siblings
description: Brown gives details about her parents, Charles Edward Martin and Hattie Geyer, including her mother's years at the Del Monte cannery in Lewiston and hospital work, and her father's jobs at the cannery, a smelter mill and a junkyard. She names her siblings Georgetta, John and Paul, and tells of an older sister who died of diphtheria and an older brother who drowned at age nine in a mining pit.

title: Husband and children
description: Brown identifies her husband Gifford Brown, born 1906 in Teakean, married in Lewiston in 1928, a retired farmer. She names their four children, Arlene, Viola, Mary Anne and Billy, giving birthplaces, years and current occupations, and compares home births with later hospital births in Orofino.

title: Skills; crafts; canning; applesauce
description: Brown lists her skills and hobbies: cooking, sewing, crocheting, embroidery, playing piano and giving music lessons, plus three teenage years working at the cannery. She describes making crafts for fairs and winning blue ribbons, then trades advice with Bush on keeping applesauce white using salt water.

title: Rural living; farm and housework; food storage
description: Brown weighs the pros and cons of rural life, saying farm chores keep children out of mischief but worrying about winter distance from doctors. She describes working alongside her husband milking cows and driving tractor, baking from scratch, smoking pork, canning meat, and the well-stocked cellar her son still misses.

title: Wood stoves; childhood work and accident
description: Brown and Bush reminisce about cooking on wood stoves and warming ovens. Brown then recalls her childhood in Clarkston caring for her brothers and preparing meals from age nine while her parents worked, her mother sewing to pay for her music lessons, and the day she was badly burned lighting the cook stove.

title: Courtship
description: Brown describes meeting Gifford Brown as the new girl at Teakean, courting over a couple of years including a horseback ride to a dance where her parents chaperoned, and his proposal as they walked home that night.

title: Marriage; in-law relationships; childbearing
description: Leah Brown discusses her marriage to a Teakean farmer, her initial jealousy, and the reasons for marrying. She describes her difficult relationship with her mother-in-law, a pioneer settler who initially rejected her, and how Leah eventually cared for her for twenty years. Leah also talks about her pregnancies, including two miscarriages and the difficult birth of her son Billy after extended bed rest.

title: Grandchildren's futures; health problems; caregiving
description: Leah assesses the futures of her various grandchildren, noting concerns about divorce, disability, and substance abuse among some, while praising others. She reveals her own health crisis, open heart surgery four years prior, and her husband's cancer diagnosis. Leah expresses gratitude for their children's care, especially a daughter who moved nearby specifically to help them.

title: Recreation; wedding memories
description: Leah describes daily life with her husband, including watching television shows like Hee Haw, Lawrence Welk, and westerns, along with her constant handwork like crocheting and sewing. She recalls her simple wedding in a blue dress bought by Gifford, the lack of a honeymoon, and her mother-in-law's refusal to attend the dinner.

title: Financial crisis; community belonging
description: Leah recounts a 1949 crisis when her husband was hospitalized for twenty-one days and she had to manage the ranch alone with help from neighbors. She reflects on feeling socially excluded in Teakean for years because they were small farmers who couldn't afford nice clothes, including Jansen sweaters that determined social status in high school.

title: Schools; education changes
description: Leah discusses the local schools her children attended, including walking to the schoolhouse by the Grange Hall and later bussing to Cavendish after consolidation. She laments the loss of community schools and worries about modern influences like drugs and drinking, while supporting young mothers fighting to keep the local school open.

title: Parenting advice; retirement finances
description: Leah offers advice on raising children with a strong work ethic, using her son's example of earning money for his own car at age twelve. She explains their retirement finances, relying on Social Security, Medicare, and income from selling land to their son, while maintaining self-sufficiency through gardening, canning, and raising meat.

title: Media; religion; marital dynamics
description: Leah lists her reading materials, including Ladies Home Journal and the Bible, and discusses her church attendance at Cream Ridge, which has declined due to illness and weather. She contrasts her worrying nature with her husband's stronger faith, and reflects on her deferential role in marriage, regretting that she didn't assert herself more in decision-making.

title: Life regrets; advice for youth
description: Leah expresses regret about not completing high school and learning typing and shorthand, and shares her love of music, including playing piano and singing at community events. She advises young people to travel and pursue opportunities while young, as she and her husband are now too ill to realize their own travel dreams.
